mechanism: A grid and recovery bot opens a ladder of positions against the trend and adds size as price moves away, closing everything when price returns to a small profit target. Most days the price oscillates back, so the daily result is green by construction. The loss sits in the tail: a sustained trend exhausts margin and the whole stack closes at once, so one day wipes out months of small wins.
claim: A 159 dollar MT5 bot for gold shows a green day on a reel and implies steady profit.
verdict_question: In a simulated martingale grid on a random walk, what share of days are green and how deep is the worst single-day loss relative to the average win?
probe_title: Martingale grid: what share of simulated days are green, and how big is the worst day versus the average win?
one_line: A grid bot is green most days by design; the cost is one trend day that erases months, and a short simulation shows the ratio.
idea_why: Selling many small wins against rare large losses looks profitable until the tail arrives, and sizing up into losses makes ruin likely.
breakdown: Write a small Python simulator of a grid with fixed spacing and a size multiplier, run it over random-walk and trending price paths, and record daily win rate, worst day and time to ruin at a fixed margin. Optionally run it on public hourly gold or BTC history to see real trend days. Compare the equity curve to buy and hold. No person is needed; the output is a chart of win rate against the single worst day.
tools_have: Claude Code with skills and sub-agents

mechanism: A malicious build of the official Claude Code VS Code extension was published to the Cursor marketplace (an Open VSX style registry), reportedly with a remote access payload. The route is a compromised publisher account or release pipeline, so editors that auto-update pulled the bad version. Yanking the version from the registry does not clean machines that already installed it.
claim: A backdoored Claude Code extension appeared on the Cursor marketplace; the page reports over 27 million installs of the extension overall.
why_not_testable: Running the compromised package would be unsafe and the affected version is yanked.
one_line: A backdoored copy of the Claude Code extension reached Cursor's marketplace, and yanking it does not clean machines that already updated.
idea_why: Registry supply chain compromise through auto-update is a well-known real attack path.
breakdown: Defence is to pin extension versions, disable auto-update on agent machines, and list installed extensions against a known-good hash list. Proteus can read the vendor notice and the extensions folder for the installed version, checking only metadata. A hired person would run an incident review of developer machines if any took the update.

mechanism: A Claude Code or Codex plugin has the model read a repo and write a graph of parts, files and web requests with plain-English names. Frontend calls are matched to server endpoints by static analysis, including across repos. A health check flags secrets, unauthenticated endpoints, unused files and oversized files. Updates re-read only changed files and the map is a local HTML page.

why_not_testable: The map is built by model calls inside a Claude session, so there is no keyless deterministic slice to verdict tonight.

one_line: Floorplan has an AI agent draw a clickable plain-English map of a codebase, matching frontend requests to server endpoints.
idea_why: Model-drawn architecture maps are useful if the connections are checked against the real import graph.
breakdown: Install the plugin in Claude Code, run it on a mid-size Proteus subfolder such as bin/, then compare its drawn connections against a plain grep of imports to count missed or invented links. The sound part is the static endpoint matching; the risky part is the model naming. A reviewer would spot-check twenty edges by hand.

mechanism: The talk splits agent memory in two: exact facts go in a SQL database queried for rows, and fuzzy understanding goes in a vector store searched by embedding similarity. A managed memory bank reads past sessions, extracts memories with a model and updates them over time. Short-term session context is treated like RAM and discarded unless promoted.
claim: Long-term agent memory needs a structured store for facts and a vector store for meaning, kept separate.
why_not_testable: Embedding search needs a model or key and there is no local LLM tonight.
one_line: Google's memory talk says keep facts in SQL and meaning in a vector store, and promote only what survives the session.
idea_why: Separating exact lookups from similarity recall matches how memory files and an index already work here.
breakdown: Proteus already keeps facts as files and an index. A step up would be a SQLite table for exact facts with dates plus a small embedding index for notes, with a nightly pass promoting items from run logs. mechanism: The reel ranks ten trading concepts with invented percentages, and claims moving-average bots never profit. The testable core is a moving-average crossover rule applied to price history. Its profit depends on regime: it gains in persistent trends and loses to whipsaw in ranges, net of fees.
claim: Order flow ranks first and MACD last, and moving-average bots never make money.
verdict_question: Does a 20/50 moving-average crossover on public daily BTC data beat buy and hold after 0.1 percent fees, and in what share of years?
probe_title: Moving-average crossover: does a 20/50 rule beat buy and hold after fees on public daily BTC history?
one_line: A reel says moving-average bots never profit; a fee-adjusted backtest on public data gives a number instead.
idea_why: The claim is checkable, and the likely answer is regime-dependent rather than never.
breakdown: Pull daily candles from a public exchange endpoint, code the crossover with a fee per switch, and compute return, drawdown and per-year win share against buy and hold. Run a few parameter pairs and report all of them to avoid picking the best. No hired work needed.

A provenance plane plants credentials and watches for later model-mediated use of them, showing attackers feed stolen keys into LLMs.

needs: a public server and the paper's code if released

idea_why: Static-response honeypots with canary credentials are a cheap, established way to measure scanning.

mechanism: A shop advertises free goods and charges only shipping, set at the real price of cheap dropshipped items. A fake closure story creates urgency, then the domain lapses and the operator relaunches under a new name. Detection signals are a young domain, an anonymous registered-agent address, near-identical sibling sites, and review sites full of shipping complaints.
claim: Free jewellery after 46 years of trading, pay shipping only.
verdict_question: Does public RDAP data show the domain registered in 2026, and how many other domains share its nameservers or registrant detail?

one_line: Free-with-shipping closure shops give themselves away in public registration data: young domains, shell agents and repeated relaunches.
idea_why: As a detection method, registration age and shared infrastructure are real, cheap fraud signals.
breakdown: Query RDAP for the domain, record creation date, registrar and nameservers, then check public certificate transparency logs for sibling hostnames. Score the signals and note which are hard to fake. This records how the pattern is caught and nothing more. No hired work needed.

mechanism: A Hyperliquid HIP-3 deployer lists perps on pump.fun graduates. The manager pulls graduates and checks holders every 10 minutes and assigns tiers by market cap hold time. The oracle takes the median of three Solana price sources every 3 seconds, smooths it with an EMA and freezes on bad data. A market maker quotes both sides, skewed against its position.
claim: A GRAD index perp from $500K market cap, and own perps for coins that hold $500K for a day, with 2x leverage.

idea_why: A median oracle is sound, but thin pools can still be moved against it, which the data would show.
